name: Benzoyl peroxide

card.summary: The over-the-counter acne staple with a strong guideline recommendation and decades of trials; the main trade-off is dryness and irritation.
card.aka: BPO, benzoyl peroxide wash or gel (e.g. 2.5%, 5%, 10%)
card.note: Can irritate and dry skin, bleach fabric and hair, and is more irritating when combined with other topical actives.

quick.overview:
Benzoyl peroxide is a topical antibacterial and keratolytic agent sold in washes, creams and gels, mostly for acne. It is available over the counter in several strengths and is also found in prescription combinations with adapalene or clindamycin.

In the 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline it receives a strong recommendation. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a cheap acne product, and some posters also describe using it on the body to reduce odor, a use that has little published support in the published literature.
quick.mechanism: It releases oxygen radicals that act against Cutibacterium acnes, the skin bacterium involved in acne, and it has a peeling (keratolytic) effect that helps unclog pores.
quick.risks: Dryness, peeling, redness and stinging are the most commonly reported effects, and product labels advise that irritation is more likely when another topical acne medicine is used at the same time. It can bleach fabric. Animal studies from 1981 reported tumour-promoting activity in mice under experimental conditions; the clinical relevance is not established in the published literature.

lead: Benzoyl peroxide (BPO) is an organic peroxide used topically for acne vulgaris and sold over the counter in washes, creams, gels and leave-on products, as well as in prescription combination products [1][2]. It acts as an antibacterial and keratolytic agent [1].

The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline for acne management makes strong recommendations for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline [3]. A JAMA review lists benzoyl peroxide among first-line topical therapies [4], and a 2022 network meta-analysis found a combined retinoid and benzoyl peroxide to be the most effective topical option for mild-to-moderate acne among those assessed [6].

In looksmaxxing communities, benzoyl peroxide is discussed as an inexpensive acne product, particularly during testosterone or steroid use, and some users promote it for reducing body odor [22][24][26]. No trial found tests it for odor.

paras: Benzoyl peroxide is used for acne vulgaris, and product labels describe it as penetrating pores to help clear and prevent blemishes and blackheads [2]. Dermatology literature also lists it among topical options for rosacea and mentions use against seborrheic dermatitis and pitted keratolysis, although the strength of evidence differs between these conditions [13][7][1].
It is also used in clinical settings to reduce skin colonization with Cutibacterium acnes before certain surgeries, as shown by registered trials in shoulder and spine surgery [17][20].

A Delphi consensus of 62 dermatologists reached agreement that benzoyl peroxide is among the ingredients recommended for acne and oily skin [5]. Beyond acne, forum users report using benzoyl peroxide washes on the armpits and back to reduce body odor by reducing skin bacteria [22]. The published literature contain no trial of that use; a registered trial of benzoyl peroxide for foot odor was withdrawn [18].

A 2022 network meta-analysis of 179 randomized trials with about 35,000 observations found that for mild-to-moderate acne, the most effective topical pharmacological option was a combination of a retinoid with benzoyl peroxide [6]. A 2000 randomized trial of 107 patients compared blue and red light phototherapy with 5% benzoyl peroxide cream and a control light [15].

Phase III trials of adapalene/benzoyl peroxide gel enrolled 1,670 and 452 people with acne vulgaris, and a phase II trial tested a fixed-dose triple combination of clindamycin, benzoyl peroxide and adapalene in moderate-to-severe acne [21][19][10]. Older clinical reports from 1966 and 1980 describe benzoyl peroxide, including with sulfur, in acne management [12][11].

Skin-care adjuncts such as ceramide and niacinamide moisturizers have been studied alongside anti-acne treatment for barrier support and tolerability [8][9]. A systematic review of antibiotic resistance in acne described rising resistance to topical and oral antibiotics, which is a reason guidelines mention combining antibiotics with other agents [16][3].

The product label for a benzoyl peroxide cleanser says it is for external use only, warns to avoid the eyes, and states that skin irritation and dryness are more likely when another topical acne medicine is used at the same time [2]. Encyclopedic summaries list dryness, peeling, redness, burning, stinging, itching and scaling as typical effects [1].

In a 1981 mouse study, benzoyl peroxide promoted skin tumours after prior application of a known initiator, and was not active alone as a carcinogen or initiator [14]. This was an animal experiment, and its relevance to people using acne products was not assessed in that paper.
Forum users describe drying, redness and flaking with leave-on gels, and recommend lower strengths for the face [23].

According to an encyclopedic summary, benzoyl peroxide was first deliberately synthesized by the British chemist B. C. Brodie in 1858 and later used industrially as a polymerization initiator and as a flour-bleaching agent [1]. The same source describes its dermatological use beginning in the 1930s and OTC acne availability from 1960 [1]. These dates come from a single AI-generated summary and are not independently verified here. A 1966 report in the Canadian Medical Association Journal discussed benzoyl peroxide with sulfur as a foundation for acne management [12].

On looksmax.org, threads ask which strength to buy, with replies noting that 5% is commonly suggested for the face and 10% for the body because leave-on gels can dry skin [23]. One thread frames benzoyl peroxide washes as a 'softmax' for body odor [22].

On T Nation, users discussing acne during testosterone therapy or steroid use mention benzoyl peroxide washes alongside salicylic acid products and sometimes while waiting for a dermatologist's isotretinoin prescription [24][26][27]. Others note it is less suited to nodular or cystic acne [25].

timeline.event: B. C. Brodie first synthesizes benzoyl peroxide, per an encyclopedic summary [1].
A Canadian Medical Association Journal paper discusses benzoyl peroxide and sulfur for acne [12].
A mouse study reports tumour-promoting activity of topical benzoyl peroxide under experimental conditions [14].
A network meta-analysis finds retinoid plus benzoyl peroxide to be the most effective topical option assessed for mild-to-moderate acne [6].
The AAD acne guideline gives benzoyl peroxide a strong recommendation [3].

lore.intro: Benzoyl peroxide is discussed in these communities as a routine acne product and, in one prominent thread, as a body-odor aid [22][23].

claims.claim: Benzoyl peroxide washes reduce body odor.
claims.believers: One poster says it kills the bacteria that break sweat down and recommends applying a BPO wash to the armpits and back every second or third day [22].
claims.experts: No published study in the published literature tests it for body odor; a registered foot-odor trial was withdrawn [18].

claims.believers: Forum users treat it as an inexpensive staple, though some describe it as only suited to mild acne or whiteheads [23][25][28].
claims.experts: Guidelines give it a strong recommendation and trials show it is effective, especially combined with a retinoid [3][6].

claims.believers: Some posters ask for 10% for quicker results [23].
claims.experts: The published literature do not compare strengths; labels and users note irritation and dryness risk [2][23].

claims.claim: Benzoyl peroxide dries and irritates the skin.
claims.believers: Users report red, flaky skin, especially with leave-on gels [23].
claims.experts: Product labels and dermatology summaries list dryness and irritation as common, particularly with other acne products [2][1].
